prompt: Why should web servers behind a load balancer be stateless?

options.text: It removes the need for a database
Any server can handle any request, so servers can be added or removed freely

explanation: Stateless web servers do not keep essential user state only in local memory. Store sessions or durable data in a shared service so another instance can handle the next request. Then adding, replacing or losing a web server does not lose that state. Stateless does not mean the whole system has no state: it moves that responsibility to a store whose capacity and availability you must also design.

scenario: Your single Postgres primary is at 90% CPU, almost entirely from writes. Reads already go to three replicas.
prompt: What gives the quickest short-term relief?

options.text: Move the primary to a bigger machine (vertical scaling)
Put a CDN in front of the API

explanation: Measure the saturated resource before scaling. This primary is busy with writes, so read replicas, a CDN and more API servers do not remove its write work. A larger primary is the quickest short-term capacity increase among these options. It has a ceiling, though. Follow up by reducing unnecessary writes, batching compatible work, or planning partitioning if sustained growth will exceed one machine.

scenario: You spread cache keys across N nodes with hash(key) % N. Adding one node to handle growth causes almost every key to move, and the hit rate collapses.
prompt: What fixes this?

options.text: Consistent hashing, so adding a node moves only about 1/N of the keys
Increase the TTL on all keys
Replicate every key to every node

explanation: Modulo placement depends on the node count: changing N changes many keys' destinations, causing cold-cache misses. Consistent hashing assigns keys and nodes positions on a ring, so adding a node moves only part of the keyspace. That limits disruption during growth. It does not automatically distribute hot keys evenly; virtual nodes can improve balance, while a single extremely popular key may need additional treatment.

scenario: Traffic doubled and p99 latency went from 80ms to 2s. The API tier autoscaled to 12 instances.
prompt: Tap the bottleneck.
explanation: Trace the work each request must perform. All 12 API instances still depend on one session store capped at 5k operations per second. That shared store limits throughput regardless of spare API capacity. Scaling the API can increase the queue of work waiting there. Measure the store, then reduce accesses, distribute session data or increase its capacity. Scale the limiting tier rather than the tier easiest to duplicate.

scenario: Traffic triples every evening and drops to almost nothing overnight.
prompt: What handles this most cost-effectively?

options.text: Buy enough servers for the evening peak and run them all day
An autoscaling group that adds and removes instances based on load

explanation: Autoscaling adjusts the number of instances as demand changes. It avoids paying for evening peak capacity all night, while allowing more capacity during the rush. The scaling signal must match the workload, and new instances take time to start. Predictable peaks may benefit from scheduled scale-out before traffic arrives. A fixed oversized fleet wastes capacity; one large instance also leaves a failure and growth limit.

scenario: One of four servers behind a load balancer crashed. Now about 25% of requests fail.
prompt: Which load balancer feature prevents this?

options.text: Health checks that stop routing to unhealthy instances

explanation: A load balancer needs a current list of usable backends. With four equal backends and no failure detection, about one request in four still goes to the crashed server. Health checks remove that backend until it recovers. They reduce failures after detection, not necessarily the first failed request. Set thresholds carefully so a brief shared dependency failure does not incorrectly eject every otherwise healthy instance.

prompt: Put the steps of adding a new server to a live pool, with zero downtime, in order.

options.text: Launch the instance from the current image
Wait until it passes the load balancer health check
Load balancer starts routing traffic to it
Watch error rate and latency for the new instance

explanation: A running process is not necessarily ready for users. Start the server, let its initialization finish, verify readiness, then admit traffic and monitor real requests. This order prevents requests reaching an instance before it can serve them. Monitoring afterward matters because a shallow health check may miss failures under load. During replacement, also drain the old instance's in-flight requests before stopping it.

scenario: Users in Europe see 400ms page loads. Your servers are in the US, and most of each page is images, CSS and JavaScript.
prompt: What is the best fix?

options.text: Serve static assets from a CDN with European edge locations

explanation: Most transferred bytes are reusable static assets, and users are far from the origin. A CDN caches those assets near European users, avoiding repeated transatlantic transfers. More US API servers would add processing capacity but would not remove the network distance. Keep origin handling for requests that need it, and use cache policies or versioned URLs so changed assets refresh correctly.

scenario: To avoid a shared session store, you enabled sticky sessions so each user always lands on the same server.
prompt: What problem does this cause as you scale?

options.text: Load becomes uneven, and users lose their session when their server dies

explanation: Sticky sessions bind each user to a particular backend. That makes local sessions convenient, but prevents free balancing: heavy users can overload one server while new servers sit idle. Losing a backend also loses sessions kept only there. Moving essential session state to a shared, reliable store lets any healthy backend serve a user. That shared store then needs its own capacity and availability plan.

scenario: Photo uploads have become very slow. The API autoscaled to 10 instances but each sits at 15% CPU.
prompt: Tap the bottleneck.
explanation: Low API CPU does not imply spare end-to-end capacity. Every upload still crosses the same file server's saturated network link, so ten APIs cannot make uploads faster. Direct uploads to object storage remove that shared data path from the API tier. Use narrowly scoped, short-lived signed URLs and validate completion before processing the file. Diagnose network and storage limits as well as CPU.

prompt: Which probe controls whether a Pod receives normal Service traffic?
explanation: A failing readiness probe marks the Pod unready for Service traffic. Liveness instead helps decide whether a container needs restarting. Source: [Kubernetes probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/probes/)

prompt: Order the simplified CPU-based HPA control loop.

options.text: Read CPU utilization for the current eligible Pods
Calculate desired replicas from current utilization and target
Update the workload replica count within configured bounds
The workload controller creates or removes Pods

explanation: HPA observes metrics, computes desired replicas relative to the target, then updates the scale target. Controllers create the resulting Pods. Source: [Kubernetes HPA](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale/)

prompt: What must be fixed for utilization-based CPU autoscaling?
scenario: A CPU-utilization HPA cannot evaluate some Pods. Relevant sidecar containers have neither CPU requests nor CPU limits.

options.text: Only increase the container image size
Configure a longer HTTP cache TTL
Set appropriate CPU requests for the relevant containers

explanation: CPU utilization is measured relative to requested CPU. If the relevant containers lack requests, HPA cannot calculate that Pod’s utilization for this metric. Source: [Kubernetes HPA](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale/)

prompt: What does this PodDisruptionBudget constrain?
scenario: A three-replica Deployment has minAvailable: 2. An operator performs a voluntary drain using the eviction API.

options.text: All application releases regardless of method
How much CPU each request may consume
Evictions that would leave fewer than two healthy replicas

explanation: A PDB limits voluntary disruptions through the eviction mechanism. It cannot prevent involuntary failures such as a node disappearing. Source: [Kubernetes PDBs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/)

prompt: Which client policy distributes RPCs across ready backend connections?
scenario: A gRPC client resolves several healthy backend addresses, but using one selected connection leaves most replicas idle.

options.text: Assign a different DNS name to every RPC

explanation: The round_robin policy cycles among ready subchannels. A policy that selects one connection can keep sending RPCs to one backend. Source: [gRPC load balancing](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/custom-load-balancing/)

prompt: Which balancing signal best matches this requirement?
scenario: A proxy handles connections with widely varying duration. Choose among equally weighted servers using their active connection counts.

options.text: Always choose the first configured server
Choose the server with the longest hostname

explanation: Least-connections sends a new request toward a server with fewer active connections, accounting for configured weights. Round-robin does not use that count. Source: [NGINX balancing](https://docs.nginx.com/nginx/admin-guide/load-balancer/http-load-balancer/)

prompt: Tap the write hotspot that the partition-key design should address.
scenario: A write-heavy event table uses one date as the partition key for every event today. Other date keys are idle; requests for today are throttled.
explanation: DynamoDB key design should distribute activity across partition keys. One extremely busy key can remain a hotspot even when other keys are idle. Source: [DynamoDB key design](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-design.html)

prompt: What fits a predictable daily surge when new instances need time to warm?
scenario: A scheduled sale begins at 09:00 every weekday. New application instances take several minutes to become useful.

options.text: Reduce the maximum replica count during the sale
Wait for the peak before starting any instances

explanation: Scheduled actions can raise desired capacity ahead of predictable demand. A schedule should account for startup time rather than waiting until the peak begins. Source: [AWS scheduled scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-scaling.html)

prompt: Tap the resource boundary that can explain the throttling.
scenario: The node has spare CPU, but the API container reaches its configured CPU limit and reports throttling. The database has low latency.
explanation: A container CPU limit can be enforced by throttling even when the node has spare CPU. Increasing replicas is a separate capacity decision. Source: [Kubernetes resources](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/)

prompt: Order an ALB slow-start target’s transition to normal traffic weight.
scenario: An existing healthy target already serves traffic. A newly registered target needs warm caches. Round-robin routing and ALB slow start are enabled.

options.text: Register a new target with the target group
Wait until the target passes the health checks
Gradually increase its traffic share during slow start
Use its full normal traffic share after the interval

explanation: With supported routing and slow start enabled, a newly healthy target’s traffic weight increases over the slow-start interval before reaching its full share. Source: [ALB slow start](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes.html#slow-start-mode)

prompt: What does maxUnavailable: 0 request during a Deployment rolling update?

options.text: No planned reduction below desired available replicas

explanation: maxUnavailable limits unavailable replicas during the rollout; zero is a rollout constraint, not an outage guarantee. Source: [Kubernetes Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)

prompt: With 3 desired replicas and maxSurge: 25%, what surge allowance is calculated?
explanation: Percentage surge rounds up: 25% of 3 is 0.75, giving an allowance of one extra Pod. Terminating Pods can add resource use. Source: [Kubernetes Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)

prompt: Which controller fits replicas that need stable ordinal names and per-replica storage?
explanation: StatefulSets associate stable identities and storage with replicas; replacement Pods can retain those identities. Source: [Kubernetes StatefulSets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/)

prompt: What happens to a scaled-down replica’s PVC when whenScaled is explicitly Retain?

options.text: It is retained for later use
It is deleted with the Pod
It is copied into every remaining Pod

explanation: Retain leaves the claim in place after scale-down. Storage retention is separate from the replica count. Source: [Kubernetes StatefulSets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/)
scenario: A StatefulSet uses volumeClaimTemplates and persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy.whenScaled: Retain.

prompt: What happens when an eligible new node joins a cluster covered by a DaemonSet?

options.text: The controller creates a matching Pod for that node
The fixed replica count stays unchanged
Every existing agent moves to the new node
Only a future CronJob can start an agent

explanation: A DaemonSet maintains node-local Pods on eligible nodes, including nodes added after its creation. Source: [Kubernetes DaemonSets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/daemonset/)

prompt: Tap the controller suited to keeping one log agent on each eligible node.
explanation: DaemonSets fit node-level agents. A fixed Deployment replica count does not itself ensure one agent on every eligible node. Source: [Kubernetes DaemonSets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/daemonset/)

prompt: Which Kubernetes abstraction gives clients a stable ClusterIP while backend Pods change?
explanation: A Service provides a stable access point for a changing set of matching backend Pods. Source: [Kubernetes Services](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/)

prompt: What does DNS for a selector-based headless Service normally return?
explanation: A headless Service allocates no ClusterIP. Its DNS records expose backing Pod addresses for direct client connections. Source: [Kubernetes Services](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/)
